messages.content: What problem does self-attention solve that recurrent networks struggle with?

Self-attention lets every position in a sequence directly attend to every other position in a single step, so long-range dependencies don't have to be carried forward through many sequential recurrent steps. This avoids the vanishing-gradient and long-path problems that make RNNs struggle to relate distant tokens, and it also allows much greater parallelization during training since positions aren't processed one at a time.
Why does the Transformer need positional encoding?

Self-attention has no inherent notion of token order — it treats the input as a set, not a sequence. Positional encodings inject information about each token's position into its embedding (commonly via fixed sine and cosine functions of different frequencies) so the model can still distinguish word order and relative position.
What is multi-head attention and why use multiple heads instead of one?

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections of queries, keys, and values, then concatenates the results. Different heads can learn to focus on different kinds of relationships (e.g., syntactic vs. positional patterns) at different representation subspaces, which a single attention operation with the same total dimensionality cannot capture as flexibly.
What does LoRA actually modify in a pretrained model?

LoRA freezes the original pretrained weight matrices and instead learns a low-rank decomposition of the weight update as two small matrices (A and B) added to selected layers, typically the attention projection matrices. Only these small low-rank matrices are trained, so the number of trainable parameters is a tiny fraction of the full model.
Why is LoRA more memory-efficient than full fine-tuning?

Because the base model's weights stay frozen, you don't need to store or update gradients and optimizer states for the full parameter count — only for the small low-rank adapter matrices. This drastically cuts the memory needed for optimizer states (e.g., Adam's moment estimates), which are often the dominant memory cost during fine-tuning.
Does LoRA add inference latency compared to the original model?

Not necessarily. The low-rank update matrices can be merged back into the original weight matrices after training by simple addition, producing a model with the exact same architecture and inference cost as the base model, with no extra runtime overhead.
What is the core idea behind retrieval-augmented generation?

RAG combines a parametric generator (a language model) with a non-parametric retriever that looks up relevant passages from an external knowledge source at inference time. The retrieved passages are provided as additional context to the generator, letting the model produce more grounded, up-to-date, and verifiable answers without needing all knowledge baked into its weights.
Why does RAG tend to reduce hallucination compared to a model generating from parameters alone?

Because the model is conditioned on retrieved source text rather than relying solely on facts implicitly memorized during pretraining, its answers can be grounded in and checked against that retrieved evidence, reducing the chance of confidently stating something unsupported or outdated.
What's the difference between a prototype in prototypical networks and a single support example used for comparison?

A prototype is the mean embedding of all support examples belonging to one class, giving a single representative point per class. Comparing a query to individual support examples one at a time (as in nearest-neighbor approaches) instead compares against multiple noisy points, whereas averaging into a prototype reduces sampling noise and gives a more stable decision boundary, especially with few examples per class.
How does a prototypical network classify a new query example?

The query is embedded using the same encoder used for the support set, then classified by finding the nearest class prototype in embedding space, typically using Euclidean distance, and converting the negative distances into class probabilities via a softmax.
What is episodic training in the context of few-shot learning?

Episodic training simulates the few-shot task structure during training itself: each training episode samples a small support set and query set from a subset of classes, mimicking the few-shot classification the model will face at test time, rather than training on the full dataset in one flat classification setup.
How does matching networks' approach differ from prototypical networks?

Matching networks classify a query using an attention mechanism over all individual support examples' embeddings, rather than collapsing each class to a single mean prototype. This can better handle classes with multi-modal or non-uniform embedding distributions, at the cost of being more computationally expensive at inference since every support example is compared individually.
What is the core technique GPTQ uses to quantize LLM weights post-training?

GPTQ quantizes weights layer by layer, using an approximate second-order (Hessian-based) method to determine the optimal rounding for each weight given the quantization already applied to earlier weights in the same layer, minimizing the resulting output error rather than just rounding each weight independently.
Why is post-training quantization for LLMs harder than for smaller CNNs?

LLMs have far more parameters and exhibit activation outliers in certain channels that are disproportionately important for accuracy, so naive uniform quantization schemes that work reasonably well on smaller CNNs can cause much larger accuracy degradation at low bit-widths in LLMs unless those outliers are handled carefully.
What problem does SmoothQuant address that standard weight-only quantization doesn't?

SmoothQuant targets the difficulty of quantizing activations (not just weights) in LLMs, where certain activation channels have much larger magnitude outliers than weights do. It migrates some of this quantization difficulty from activations to weights via a mathematically equivalent rescaling, making both activations and weights easier to quantize to low bit-widths with less accuracy loss.
What is knowledge distillation in one sentence?

Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic the output distribution (not just the hard labels) of a larger, already-trained teacher model, transferring the teacher's learned generalization into a more compact model.
Why does distillation use the teacher's soft probabilities instead of just its predicted class?

Soft probabilities carry extra information the teacher has learned about how classes relate to each other — e.g., how confident it is and which wrong classes are more plausible — which a single hard label discards. Training the student to match this richer soft distribution (often with a temperature-scaled softmax) transfers more of the teacher's learned structure.
What is temperature scaling in knowledge distillation and why is it used?

Temperature scaling divides the logits by a temperature value before the softmax, producing a softer probability distribution over classes. A higher temperature reveals more about the relative probabilities the teacher assigns to incorrect classes, giving the student more informative gradients than an unscaled, overly peaked distribution would.
